columns: How much land it held about 1750
rows: Very large -- most of eastern Asia

Once very large; breaking apart into smaller states by 1750
Emperor's authority weakening; regional rulers taking power
Southwest Asia, southeastern Europe, and North Africa
Large -- reaching across three continents; shrinking at the edges
Shogun; tight control over the lords and over travel
Small next to the great land empires

stimulus.content: The Tokugawa shogunate realized the importance of maintaining contact with distant provinces within Japan. The Tokaido was its most important highway. . . . Government messengers had priority over any other type of traveler. They had first access to ferries at river crossings along the way, and could freely pass government road barriers at all times of the day or night. Private citizens were not allowed to travel at night; a series of barriers and checkpoints along the road kept them from doing so.
stimulus.citation: Source: Patricia J. Graham, "The Political and Economic Importance of the Tokaido," Tokaido: Adventures on the Road in Old Japan, University of Kansas Spencer Museum of Art (adapted), from the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, January 2012

provenance.note: NYSED-released passage reaching this desk through New Visions. Teach freely, do not sell.

reps.exemplar: This document matches Power & Its Abuse: the road wasn't just for travel, it was a tool the shogunate used to control who could move, when, and how fast -- government messengers got total freedom while ordinary people were boxed in by curfews and checkpoints.
reps.compare_focus: Read the road as control, not just transportation, before naming the umbrella.
compare_checklist: Did I name one of the Six Umbrellas exactly?
Did I use a specific detail from the document, not just the general topic (a road)?
Did I explain why that detail fits the umbrella, not just assert that it does?
